assessment.nobel_worthiness: The optical lattice clock, built on Katori's magic-wavelength proposal, reaches fractional uncertainties near 1e-18 and turns time into the most precisely measured quantity in physics. It is a clean, unexpected-in-ambition route past the microwave standard, and it opens tests of fundamental constants, relativistic redshift over millimetres and a redefinition of the second. Precision and robust theory-experiment agreement are what I value most.
assessment.attribution: Katori conceived the magic-wavelength lattice trapping scheme and built early strontium clocks; Jun Ye's group brought the systematic uncertainty to the 1e-18 level and demonstrated the many-body clock. The two-name credit is a fair and compact configuration. Others (Hall and Hansch with the comb, earlier prized; Ludlow, Bloom, Kitagawa) are part of the story but not the core.
assessment.maturity: Confirmed by multiple independent laboratories (JILA, RIKEN/Tokyo, PTB, NIST, SYRTE, others) with mutual comparisons at 1e-18. The interpretation is stable and recognition is timely, as the redefinition of the second is under discussion.
uncertainties: Fair division of credit with ion-clock work (Wineland-related) and with frequency-comb pioneers already honoured is not fully settled.
Credit to Pierre Lemonde, Peik and others for the proposal history is not covered by the supplied names.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The prediction of the time-reversal-invariant quantum spin Hall state and Z2 topological insulators, and its realisation in HgTe wells, revealed a genuinely new class of matter where bulk topology dictates protected surface or edge conduction. It changed how we classify phases beyond symmetry breaking and has had broad consequences across condensed matter physics, although it is outside my own field and I defer to colleagues there.
assessment.attribution: Kane and Mele made the decisive theoretical prediction and Z2 classification; Molenkamp's group delivered the HgTe quantum well experiment with Bernevig-Hughes-Zhang's proposal. Zahid Hasan's ARPES work on the 3D materials is an additional strong claim, so a Kane, Mele and Molenkamp trio would leave out Hasan, and the allocation between 2D and 3D discoveries and the missing names (Bernevig, Zhang, Fu) is a real difficulty.
assessment.maturity: Experimentally confirmed repeatedly in HgTe, InAs/GaSb and Bi-based 3D materials; the framework is a stable part of the field. Recognition is mature and arguably overdue.
uncertainties: Omission of Hasan or Bernevig and Zhang could be contested.
Practical applications remain modest, though the basic discovery stands without them.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Ultracold atoms in optical lattices have turned the Hubbard model from a theoretical abstraction into a tunable laboratory system, with direct observation of the superfluid to Mott insulator transition and single-site-resolved quantum gas microscopy. This tells us how many-body quantum states form, and one can watch dynamics in time in a clean system, which I find compelling.
assessment.attribution: Jaksch-Zoller (with Cirac and Gardiner) proposed the Hubbard realisation; Greiner and Bloch performed the Mott insulator experiment, and Bloch and Greiner made the quantum gas microscopes (with Bakr and Greiner). Five credited names exceed the three-person limit, so it is hard to avoid omitting people such as Esslinger, Cirac or Jaksch.
assessment.maturity: Many laboratories have reproduced and extended the results; the field is mature and the interpretation is stable. Recognition is timely but competes with the 2001 BEC prize and other cold-atom credits.
uncertainties: Selection among Bloch, Greiner, Zoller, Cirac and Esslinger is contested.
Whether quantum simulation has produced a result beyond classical computation is still being debated.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The Cirac-Zoller proposal for quantum gates with trapped ions and the subsequent experimental realisation of entangling gates and small quantum algorithms laid the foundation for controllable quantum systems with few-body precision. Atomic physics at its best, with pristine control of individual quantum systems and a clear route to scaled-up devices.
assessment.attribution: Cirac and Zoller made the original gate proposal; Blatt's group demonstrated key operations such as teleportation and the Innsbruck experiments. Wineland and Monroe are well known for the first experimental gate and for NIST work and Wineland already received the 2012 prize; Monroe and Kim are not among the credited names, so attribution would be incomplete.
assessment.maturity: Replicated across many laboratories and now in commercial devices; very mature. Slight risk that part of the recognition was already covered by the 2012 prize for individual quantum systems.
uncertainties: Overlap with the 2012 prize and with the cold-atom candidate B044 for Cirac and Zoller.
Missing credit for Monroe, Kim and Wineland's gate demonstration.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The titanium-sapphire gain medium and passive mode-locking via Kerr-lens and semiconductor saturable absorber mirrors made femtosecond lasers practical and are the enabling technology of attosecond science, ultrafast spectroscopy and frequency combs. The discovery was a step in laser physics with large downstream effects, though I recognise it is nearer to invention than to discovery about nature.
assessment.attribution: Moulton invented the Ti:sapphire laser; Sibbett's group demonstrated Kerr-lens mode-locking and Keller invented SESAM mode-locking. The three-name configuration is reasonable. I know Keller's group and have collaborated with it, and should note that bias openly.
assessment.maturity: Fully mature and ubiquitous, with decades of independent use. Recognition is arguably late; some of the field was honoured in 2018 (chirped pulse amplification) and 2023 (attosecond pulses).
uncertainties: Whether the committee views it as an invention-type prize with sufficient fundamental content.
Kerr-lens mode-locking credit (Sibbett, Spence, Kean) is shared and the supplied name list may not cover everything.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Circuit QED brings strong light-matter coupling to superconducting circuits, allowing single-photon and qubit control, dispersive readout and the architecture used in most superconducting quantum processors. It has a clear link to my interest in how quantum behaviour appears in engineered systems, though it follows closely after the 2025 prize for macroscopic quantum tunnelling in circuits.
assessment.attribution: Blais, Girvin and Schoelkopf with Huang, Majer and Wallraff wrote the circuit QED proposal and Wallraff, Schoelkopf and colleagues realised strong coupling in 2004. Girvin is a fourth principal; choosing three from four credited names requires leaving out a deserving person.
assessment.maturity: Extensively reproduced and now the basis of industry platforms; mature. Timing is complicated by the 2025 prize recognising related superconducting circuits work.
uncertainties: Close proximity to the 2025 prize may reduce the probability of recognition.
Allocation among Blais, Girvin, Schoelkopf and Wallraff is unresolved.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Quantised conductance in ballistic point contacts was an unexpected and beautifully simple demonstration that electrical conductance is quantised in units of 2e^2/h, and it underlies the Landauer picture of transport in mesoscopic systems. It is a clear example of the quantum-to-classical boundary seen in a transistor-like device.
assessment.attribution: Two groups reported the effect independently in 1988: van Wees, van Houten and colleagues at Delft/Philips, and Wharam, Pepper and colleagues at Cambridge. The supplied names are credible, but Wharam and Ritchie are not included and the Delft-Cambridge split would need care.
assessment.maturity: Reproduced everywhere and now textbook; the interpretation is stable. The recognition is very late rather than premature and so the prize timing is less pressing.
uncertainties: Dual priority between Delft and Cambridge and omitted co-authors.
Whether the committee judges this more as a mesoscopic milestone than a transformative discovery.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The Aharonov-Bohm effect and the Berry phase show that potentials and geometry have physical consequences in quantum mechanics, shaping the foundation of gauge theory, topological band theory and adiabatic dynamics. This is fundamental understanding of a very high order and the kind of surprise about nature I most admire.
assessment.attribution: Aharonov and Bohm (1959) and Berry (1984) are separate discoveries; Bohm died in 1992 and cannot be recognised, and Aharonov-Casher and Pancharatnam are linked. A prize for Berry alone or Berry and Aharonov would need an explicit statement that the conceptual unity justifies a joint recognition.
assessment.maturity: Experimentally confirmed (Chambers, Tonomura, many Berry-phase observations), and entirely mature. Recognition has probably been too long delayed rather than premature.
uncertainties: The compound nature of the discovery and the deceased co-originator.
Whether the committee sees this as a coherent single prize or two different contributions.
